column2: ENGLISH

You are of age now, and so the grudgekeeper of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] takes down the Dammaz Kron and reads it to you, line by line, as it was read to your father and to his father. The wrong, the name, the day it was written. Most of the names are long dead and their debts long paid in blood. Some are not.\n\n"These are yours now," the old Dawi says. "Until they are struck out."
I will not forget a single one.
You take up every grudge your parents hold against the living.

The war is over, and Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] has come out of it the worse. [From.GetTitledName] has the better of you for now, but a Dawi does not forget and does not forgive.\n\nThe grudgekeeper sharpens a new quill. In the column for the wrong, the war. In the column for the name, [From.GetBestName]. The column for the day it is satisfied stays empty.
Write it down. In full.

A messenger of your clan brings word from your [GetFromRelation] [From.GetFirstName]: a new grudge has been written in the clan's book against [grudge_offender.GetBestName]. By the law of the ancestors it binds every Dawi of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName], you among them, until it is satisfied.
It is a matter of honour.

You open the Dammaz Kron of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName]. Its oldest pages are older than the hold, written in runes few now read, and the newest are still sharp with fresh ink. Line after line has been struck through. These have not.

You open the Dammaz Kron of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] and read down the last pages. Every line is struck through. Every wrong has been paid for. For the moment, at least, the clan owes no one and is owed nothing.\n\nIt will not last.
Close the book.
The grudge against [This.GetBestName], still unsatisfied

By [Root.Religion.GetRandomGodName], it is done. [grudge_offender.GetTitledName] has been beaten, and the grudge of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] against [grudge_offender.GetHerHim] can at last be struck out. Dawi law leaves the amends to the wronged: whatever you judge enough, and nothing [grudge_offender.GetSheHe] says about it matters.
Empty [grudge_offender.GetHerHis] treasury.
Take [grudge_offender.GetHerHis] kin as hostages.
Nothing but [grudge_offender.GetHerHis] head will do.

A letter, written in a hard square hand and sealed with a hammer:

"To [Root.GetBestName], kruti, wazzock and [Root.GetSonDaughter] of a grobi. Know that your name is written in the Book of Grudges of Clan [From.GetOnlyDynastyName], and it will stay there until the debt is paid. We have struck out grudges a thousand years old. We can wait.

[From.GetBestName]"
Let them wait, then.

The Elders of Clan [From.GetOnlyDynastyName] have met, and what they have decided is final. For the wrong you did [From.GetBestName], your own kin, you are struck from the clan. Your name is cut from its book of remembrance and written instead in its book of grudges.\n\nYou must found a clan of your own, and your children with you. The clan you were born to will never let it rest.
Then I will make a clan worth more than theirs.
The plot is out, and the name behind it with it: [From.GetBestName]. A Dawi might be fooled once by a thagi, a murderous traitor, but never twice, and never without writing it down.

One of the kin of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] is dead, and it was no accident. [From.GetBestName] is behind it, and the clan knows it. Some grudges are paid in gold. This one will be paid in blood.
Grungni curse [From.GetHerHim]. Write it down.
[From.GetTitledName] is dead, slain by [grudge_offender.GetBestName]. The priests of Gazul will see [From.GetHerHim] safe to the Hall of Ancestors. What is left to you is the debt.
The debt will be paid.

[From.GetBestName] has broken the oath of your marriage. Dawi law is clear: the one who breaks a marriage oath owes the other oathgold, a weight of it set by rank. If [From.GetSheHe] will not pay, the clan will write the grudge.
[From.GetSheHe] will pay. Surely.
[From.GetBestName] is asked to pay oathgold.

A Reckoner of Clan [From.GetOnlyDynastyName] stands before you, an old Dawi with a stone tablet under his arm. "By the law of the ancestors," he says, "the one who breaks the marriage oath owes oathgold to the other. Pay it, and the matter is closed and the tablet broken. Refuse, and the clan writes a grudge."
Very well. Here is your gold.
Not one coin, you kruti.
Clan [From.GetOnlyDynastyName] will write a grudge against you.
The Reckoner is back, and the stone tablet with him, broken neatly in two. [From.GetBestName] has paid the oathgold to the last coin, as the law requires. The matter is closed.
As it should be.

The Reckoner is back, and the stone tablet with him, whole. [From.GetBestName] has refused the oathgold. The honour of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] has been spat on, and there is only one answer to that.
So be it. Write it down.
[From.GetTitledName] was asked to stand beside you in your war, as an ally is bound to. [From.GetSheHe] has refused. In the holds that is not called caution. It is called betrayal.
Write [From.GetHerHim] into the book.
[From.GetSheHe] had [From.GetHerHis] reasons, I suppose.
A grudge against [grudge_offender.GetBestName] is written in the Book of Grudges of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName].

[grudge_offender.GetBestName] is of your own clan. [grudge_offender.GetSheHe] is cast out of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] with [grudge_offender.GetHerHis] children, and founds a clan of [grudge_offender.GetHerHis] own.
The ordinary grudges of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] against [grudge_offender.GetBestName] are struck out. A Blood Grudge stays in the book.

The grudge against [grudge_offender.GetBestName] has stood in the book long enough. By Dawi law you may send a Reckoner to demand amends, and the law says what he may ask. A slight is paid with a public apology. Any other wrong with gold, or from a Dawi a hold. But a Blood Grudge takes no gold at all: only the offender's head, or a Dawi's oath to walk the Slayer's path. If amends are made the tablet is broken and the grudge struck out. If not, it stands.
Gold, and plenty of it.
One of [grudge_offender.GetHerHis] holds.
Let it lie for now.

A Reckoner of Clan [From.GetOnlyDynastyName] stands before you with a stone tablet under his arm, the grudge against you cut into it. [From.GetTitledName] demands amends in gold. Pay, and the grudge is struck out and the tablet broken. Refuse, and it stays in [From.GetHerHis] book, and [From.GetSheHe] will come for it in [From.GetHerHis] own time.
Pay the Reckoner.
Get out.

A Reckoner of Clan [From.GetOnlyDynastyName] stands before you with a stone tablet under his arm, the grudge against you cut into it. [From.GetTitledName] demands amends in land: one of your holds, given over to [From.GetHerHim]. Give it, and the grudge is struck out. Refuse, and [From.GetSheHe] will come to take it.
Give up the hold.
Never.

The Reckoner comes back with a chest of gold from [From.GetBestName], and the tablet broken in two. The grudge is satisfied, and the grudgekeeper writes the day in the last column and draws a line through it.

The Reckoner comes back with the deeds to a hold of [From.GetBestName]'s, and the tablet broken in two. The grudge is satisfied, and the grudgekeeper writes the day in the last column and draws a line through it.
One struck out. How many more?

The Reckoner comes back with the tablet whole and an earful of insults. [From.GetBestName] will not make amends. The grudge stands, and Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] will have to settle it the old way.
Thrice-cursed [From.GetSonDaughter] of a grobi!
Send a Reckoner to [Root.GetBestName]
Send a Reckoner to demand amends from [Root.GetBestName] for the grudge of Clan [From.GetOnlyDynastyName] against [Root.GetHerHim].
Open the Book of Grudges
Read the Dammaz Kron of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName]: every wrong against the clan not yet paid for.
An Unsettled Grudge
This Dawi's clan book holds an unsettled grudge against the living. Every day they stand is a shame to the clan.
Two Unsettled Grudges
This Dawi's clan book holds two unsettled grudges against the living. Every day they stand is a shame to the clan.
Three Unsettled Grudges
This Dawi's clan book holds three unsettled grudges against the living. Every day they stand is a shame to the clan.
Four Unsettled Grudges
This Dawi's clan book holds four unsettled grudges against the living. Every day they stand is a shame to the clan.
A Book of Unsettled Grudges
This Dawi's clan book holds five or more unsettled grudges against the living. Every day they stand is a shame to the clan.

You have let your honour fall so low that the ancestors turn their faces from you, and every Dawi in the hold knows it. The law leaves you two roads.

Go to the temple of Grimnir and give yourself to the Slayer ritual: your head shaved to a crest and dyed orange, your shame tattooed into your skin, your hold, your wealth and your kin given up, and nothing left but to seek a death great enough to wash it out.

Or live on as Unbaraki, an oathbreaker, the worst thing there is in Dawi estimation.
Take me to Grimnir's temple.
I will live, and let them spit.
You become a §YSlayer§!: you give up your titles to your heir, your spouses and your wealth, and walk the Slayer's path until you find your death.
You are §YUnbaraki§!. Other Dawi will despise you, and Dawi lords may make war on you to cast you down.

[dawi_new_slayer.GetTitledFirstName] has gone to the temple of Grimnir and come out a Slayer, with the orange crest and the tattoos and an axe and nothing else. [dawi_new_slayer.GetSheHeCap] has given up everything, and so the rule of [Root.PrimaryTitle.GetName] passes to you.
May [dawi_new_slayer.GetSheHe] find the death [dawi_new_slayer.GetSheHe] seeks.

[old_slayer_king.GetTitledName] is dead, and the doom [old_slayer_king.GetSheHe] sought is not yet found. The Slayer Kings of old passed their oath down the line, father to son, each looking for the death the last one did not find.\n\nThe priests of Grimnir ask whether you will take it up.
I will take up the doom of my line.
This has gone on long enough.

[Root.GetBestName],

The beasts in [From.GetName] are dead. You are welcome. Do not thank me, I did not do it for you, and none of them was big enough.

[FromFrom.GetFirstName], Slayer
Well, that is one way to say it.

[From.GetFullName] went out after the beasts and has not come back. No one has found the body, which, with a Slayer, is a good sign: it means whatever [From.GetSheHe] fought was big enough to leave nothing. [From.GetSheHe] has found the death [From.GetSheHe] went looking for.
Rest now, Slayer. Your shame is paid.

[From.GetFullName] has gone. There is nothing left near [From.Location.GetName] worth dying to, [From.GetSheHe] says, and so [From.GetSheHe] has packed an axe and nothing else and walked out of the gate, looking for something that is.
Go well, Slayer.
[From.GetFullName] leaves for another realm.

A Slayer has turned up at your gate: [From.GetFullName], orange crest, bare chest, more tattoos than skin and an axe as long as a manling is tall. [From.GetSheHe] wants nothing from you but to know where the beasts are. Your folk are giving [From.GetHerHim] a wide berth.
[From.GetSheHe] can stay. Point [From.GetHerHim] at the beasts.
Send [From.GetHerHim] on.

A Dawi has walked into your hall, alone, half naked, with an orange crest and an axe, and the guards at the door have not stopped [From.GetHerHim]. [From.GetBestName] does not want gold or land. [From.GetSheHe] wants to kill you, or to die trying, and does not seem to mind which.
Let [From.GetHerHim] try.
OI BOSS! One of dem orange-'ead stunties, [From.GetBestName], 'as walked right in past da ladz an' sez 'e's 'ere to krump ya! 'E's got no armour an' a big axe an' 'e's LAUGHIN'!
I'M GONNA PULL OFF 'IS SHINY ORANGE 'AIR!
Master! Master! One of the dwarf-things, the mad orange-fur kind, [From.GetBestName], it walk-walked right into your burrow! It killed the guard-rats! It wants to murder-kill you, yes-yes!
Then kill-kill it, quick!

Word comes up from the border watch-posts: a patrol led by [dawi_hero.GetTitledFirstName] ran into a band of greenskins three times its number in the high passes, held the narrow way behind a wall of shields, and broke them. [dawi_hero.GetFirstName] was in the front rank the whole time, they say, and left a trail of grobi behind [dawi_hero.GetHerHim] like a miner leaves spoil.
Write it in the Book of Remembrance.
I could have done as well.

Word comes up from the border watch-posts, and it is not good. A patrol led by [dawi_coward.GetTitledFirstName] met the enemy in the high passes, and [dawi_coward.GetFirstName] ran, and left [dawi_coward.GetHerHis] kin to hold the way alone. Some of them did not come back.\n\nA Dawi who flees the enemies of the hold shames the clan back to the first ancestor.
That was ill done.
Lock [dawi_coward.GetHerHim] up until the Elders judge it.
Get [dawi_coward.GetHerHim] out of my hold.

Below every hold the old tunnels go on further than any map: worked-out seams, fallen halls, the roads of holds that are gone. The tunnel fighters go down there every season, to clear out the grobi and see what the deeps will give up. They have room for one more.
Hand me a lamp.
The lamps show a crack in the tunnel wall that is not on any map, and beyond it a passage going down. The air coming up out of it is old and dry. Somebody cut this, a long time ago.
We will not get rich standing here. In we go.
Better to leave it alone.

At the end of the passage the lamplight catches on the wall, and the wall catches it back: a seam the old miners missed, thick as your arm. You chip out a pocketful of it as proof and mark the place on the map, and for once nobody grumbles about the climb back.
One for me, one for the clan.

The passage ends in a blank wall, and behind you somebody shouts a warning that is cut off short. It is a trap, and the things that set it are coming down the passage behind you. There is no way out but through them.
Fight for our lives!

Somewhere ahead in the dark a gong is beaten, and then the tunnel fills with shrieking. Night goblins, hundreds of them, pouring out of the side passages with their hoods up and their knives out. The tunnel fighters close up shoulder to shoulder and lock their shields.
Into the shield wall! For Grimnir and the ancestors!
Leave this to the tunnel fighters.
You stay at the back, behind the shields, and let the veterans do the work. They do it well. Afterwards nobody says anything about where you stood. Nobody needs to.
Well fought, lads. Get us out of here.

They are only grobi when all is said and done. The shield wall holds, the axes rise and fall, and in the end the survivors run squealing back into the dark and leave their dead in heaps. You did your share of that and more.
You should see me when I am angry.

You fight, and they keep coming, more of them than there are stones in the wall. The shield wall bends back, and back again. There is nothing for it but to give ground, step by step, and hope the tunnel behind you is still clear.
Fall back! Keep the shields up!

Deep below the hold the tunnel opens into a hall nobody has stood in for a thousand years. Pillars carved with the faces of ancestors, a sealed door at the far end, runes over it half worn away. The tunnel fighters do not want to go any closer. They say the dead do not like to be disturbed.
I will go in myself. We have to know what this was.
Leave it. It is not ours to disturb.

The runes over the door are not ones you know, and you kick it open anyway. Inside is a stone coffin and the carved likeness of an old Dawi with his hands on an axe. You have broken into some clan's tomb, and there is no getting the seal back.
Valaya forgive me.

You know these runes. This is an old shrine of Grungni, the Ancestor God of the mine, from the days of the first holds. You say the old words in the dark, and then gather up what the priests left behind, to take home where it will be safe.

You know these runes. This is an old shrine of Grungni, the Ancestor God of the mine, from the days of the first holds. You say the old words in the dark, and then gather up what the priests left behind.\n\nOn the altar lies a great hammer, its head still bright under the dust. Whoever left it here meant it to be found by kin.
Grungni be thanked.
You are in no state to go any further, and the tunnel fighters know it. They carry you back up to the light, grumbling about the weight, and leave you with the healers. Your delving is over for now.
I will be back down there before long.
Delve the Deeps
Go down into the old tunnels below the hold with the tunnel fighters, hunting for lost seams, forgotten halls and grobi.
Return from the Deeps
Come back up from the old tunnels.

The throne of the Karaz Ankor stands empty, as it has for longer than anyone likes to say aloud. The holds keep their own counsel and their own books of grudges, and the enemies of the Dawi grow fat on it.\n\nYou are old enough and great enough to call a Council of Kings, as the ancestors did, and ask them to name you High King. It will cost you dearly in renown and honour whichever way the vote goes, and a king who calls the Council and loses will not be allowed to forget it.
Send the messengers. It is time.
Not yet.
Every independent Dawi king and lord of the ancestor gods is summoned to vote. The Council gives its verdict in about six weeks.

A messenger has come from [high_king_candidate.GetTitledName], and he carries a summons no Dawi king has received in centuries: to a Council of Kings, there to name [high_king_candidate.GetFirstName] High King of the Karaz Ankor.\n\nIf [high_king_candidate.GetSheHe] wins, every king who voted for [high_king_candidate.GetHerHim] will kneel to [high_king_candidate.GetHerHim]. If not, [high_king_candidate.GetSheHe] will remember who voted against.
Let the holds stand together again.
I will not kneel to this beardling.

A letter from [From.GetTitledName]:\n\n"I will never kneel to you, pretender. You are the get of a grobi shaman and a she-troll, and the Council will see you for what you are. Come and make me, if you dare."
We will see how [From.GetSheHe] fares alone.

The Council of Kings is over and the votes are counted: [Root.dawi_council_yes.GetValue] for you, [Root.dawi_council_no.GetValue] against. The kings of the Karaz Ankor have spoken, and they have named you High King.\n\nThe crown is brought out of the vaults where it has waited all this time.

The Council of Kings is over and the votes are counted: [Root.dawi_council_yes.GetValue] for you, [Root.dawi_council_no.GetValue] against. The kings of the Karaz Ankor have spoken, and they will not have you.\n\nSome of them did stand with you. With them, you could claim the throne anyway, and make the rest kneel by the axe.
Bring the crown. Let the holds tremble.
Grumbaki fools! I will forge it myself.
Wazzoks. Some other time, then.
You take the throne of the §YKaraz Ankor§!. Every independent king who voted for you swears fealty.
You proclaim yourself High King anyway, as lord of §YDrek Ankor§!, and will have to fight for it.
Drek Ankor
Drek Ankor

[From.GetTitledName] has been crowned High King of the Karaz Ankor, with your voice among those that named [From.GetHerHim]. It is time to keep your word. You kneel before the throne and swear fealty, as your ancestors swore it to the High Kings of old.
My High King.

News from the mountains: the Dawi have a High King again. [From.GetTitledName] has been named High King of the Karaz Ankor by a Council of Kings, the first in centuries, and the holds stand together under one throne.
The greenskins will not like that.
An envoy of [From.GetTitledName], High King of the Karaz Ankor, stands before you with a demand from the throne: that you kneel, and hold your lands of the High King as the kings of old did.
I will kneel.
I kneel to no one.

The long table in the hall groans under the roast and the bread, and the brewmaster has rolled out every cask in the cellar: dark ales, pale ales, the strong stuff they keep for the Day of Remembrance. You are on your fifth flagon, and somewhere down the table a Longbeard is calling for a sixth all round.\n\nA Dawi is expected to hold his ale. Then again, nobody wants to be carried to bed in front of the whole clan.
Five more, and then we will see who is carried to bed!
I am a Dawi, not a drunkard.

[dawi_beer_host.GetTitledName] has done you the honour of a seat at [dawi_beer_host.GetHerHis] table, and the honour of a flagon of the local ale. You take a mouthful. It is thin, it is sour, and it tastes faintly of the bucket it was drawn in. Around the table the umgi are drinking it as though it were ale.
Are you trying to poison me?
Swallow it, and smile.
[dawi_beer_host.GetFirstName] will hear exactly what you think of the ale

Your guest, [From.GetTitledName], has spat a mouthful of your best ale back into the flagon, in front of the whole hall, and announced that [From.GetSheHe] has drunk better out of a mine sump. The Dawi at the table are nodding along. The rest of your court is waiting to see what you do.
Mind your manners, dwarf!
Fetch a cask of Dawi ale from the cellar.
Send to the hold for proper Dawi ale.
One cask of Dawi ale is gone from your cellar
Five casks of Dawi ale arrive. One goes straight to the table, and four go into your cellar for the next Dawi guest
[From.GetTitledName] did not take it well. A manling can brew all [From.GetHerHis] life and still not know good ale from bilge water, it seems, and does not care to be told.
Umgi.
[From.GetTitledName] took your words to heart: a cask of true Dawi ale is broached at the table, and it is everything the local stuff is not. Perhaps there is hope for the umgi yet.
Now that is ale.

After the meal the old songs are sung in the hall: the building of the first holds, the war against the elgi, the long fight against the grobi, the halls that fell and the halls that still stand. Every Dawi in the hall knows the words. You find you are singing with them.
We are the eldest of the folk, and the best.
We were greater once. We will be again.

The new ale is sour. Not a little sour: the whole brewing has turned, every cask of it, and the hold has been grumbling for a week. The brewmaster stands before you with his hat in his hands. He has brewed for your clan for a century, and you have never seen him look so old.\n\nThe brewmaster of a hold is as respected as many a king, and a brewmaster who fails his hold carries the shame of it on his own head.
Every brewer has a bad year. Here is gold for better barley.
The hold will not drink this. Let him answer for it.
Ale is ale. We will drink it.
The brewmaster shaves his head and takes the Slayer's oath at the shrine of Grimnir. He will stay at your court until he finds his death

The miners of [dawi_vein_province.GetName] have broken into a seam of gold as thick as a Longbeard's arm, running down further than their lamps can see. They came up to tell you themselves, still black with the dust of the deep galleries and grinning through their beards.
Dig it out, every last grain.
The first gold goes to the temple of Grungni.

A Dawi has wandered up out of the deep ways under [Root.Capital.GetName], filthy and half starved, with an old mining lamp still clutched in his fist. He does not know his clan or his hold, or how long he has been down there. He remembers a hall full of grobi and running. He asks for a place at your court until his memory comes back.
Of course. You are kin.
Give him bread for the road, and send him on.
The miner goes on his way to look for his own hold
The Oldest Craft

Of all the crafts of the Dawi, none is honoured more than masonry. The masons cut the great halls of the holds out of the living rock, raise the gates and walls that have held back the grobi for thousands of years, and carve the faces of the ancestors into the pillars so that no Dawi will forget them. A good wall outlives the mason who built it by ten thousand years.\n\nYou have taken up the chisel and the mallet. Your hands will be raw for a decade, and the masons of the hold will judge every stone you lay.
Glory to the Dawi, and to their stone.
You begin to learn the mason's craft. Every two years you take on a new piece of work, and good work may make you a mason of the hold
Your skill as a mason grows

You have spent a season carving a small statue of a Dawi warrior out of a block of grey stone. The axe is a little too small and the beard a little too short, but it is a Dawi, and anybody could tell it was. The masons have even nodded at it.

You have spent a season carving a small statue of a Dawi warrior out of a block of grey stone. Halfway through it, the axe arm came off with a crack. The masons say nothing, which is worse than anything they could say.
Not bad. Not bad at all.
Back to the quarry for another block.

One of the watchtowers of [Root.Capital.GetName] had a rough inner wall, and you have dressed it smooth with your own chisel. There are a few scratches if you look closely, but the stones sit true, and the tower guards have stopped snagging their cloaks on it.

One of the watchtowers of [Root.Capital.GetName] had a rough inner wall, and you set out to dress it smooth with your own chisel. You took off too much. Now the wall is rougher than before and a crack is running up from the floor, and the tower guards are looking at it nervously.
A wall to be proud of.
Get the masons to shore it up before it falls.

You have spent a season working beside the masons of the hold. They taught you how to read the grain of the stone, where to strike and where to leave well alone, and they did not laugh at you more than once or twice a day.
You have spent a season working beside the masons of the hold. They tried to teach you how to read the grain of the stone, and you tried to learn, and the both of you are glad the season is over.
I learned more in a season than in ten years of watching.
Perhaps next season.

The floor of the throne room has been uneven for as long as anyone can remember, and you have relaid it yourself, slab by slab. It is level now, from the doors to the steps of the throne, and the whole court walks over your work every day.

The floor of the throne room has been uneven for as long as anyone can remember, and you have relaid it yourself, slab by slab. It is worse now. The court walks over your work every day, and every day somebody trips.
Level as a still pool.
Nobody is to mention the floor.

The masons of the hold have been to see your latest piece of work, and the oldest of them ran his hand over it for a long time before he spoke. Then he said it would do. From a Dawi mason, there is no higher praise. You are one of them now.
I am a mason of the hold.

You have finished carving the pillars of the throne room. Runes of remembrance wind up every one of them: the names of your ancestors, the deeds of the clan, the grudges settled and the grudges still open. Any Dawi who stands in the hall can read the clan's history in the stone.

You set out to carve runes of remembrance into the pillars of the throne room, and three times your chisel slipped and opened a crack in the stone. A cracked pillar cannot carry the clan's history. New ones will have to be cut and brought up from the quarry.
Now the stone remembers.
Order new pillars from the quarry.

The gatehouse of [Root.Capital.GetName] was battered by a hundred years of sieges. You have rebuilt it stone by stone, and the new gate is set so deep in the rock that a troll could beat on it for a year and not shift it.

The gatehouse of [Root.Capital.GetName] was battered by a hundred years of sieges, and you set out to rebuild it. Halfway through the work the old arch gave way. Nobody was killed, but the gate stands open to the road, and you will have to pay sellswords to guard it until it is rebuilt.
Let them come.
Hire guards, and start again.

The battlements of [Root.Capital.GetName] are rebuilt, wider and higher than before, with new firing steps for the Quarrellers and Thunderers and a parapet that would turn a cannonball. The garrison is walking along them as if they had built them themselves.

The battlements of [Root.Capital.GetName] were to be rebuilt wider and higher than before, but a whole stretch of the new parapet came down in the first storm. The garrison is short of wall to stand on, and the work will have to be done again.
No grobi will climb these.
Pull it down and do it properly.

The spring floods have carried off the wooden bridges of [dawi_bridge_province.GetName], and the roads are cut. You could build them again, in stone this time, as the ancestors did: bridges that will outlast every flood for the next thousand years.
In stone, and better than before.
Let the umgi wade.

For a long time you have wanted to carve a statue of one of the great Ancestor Gods for the hall. Grimnir the Fearless, with his two axes, who went north into the Chaos Wastes to close the gate and never came back. Grungni, who taught the Dawi to mine and to work metal. Or Valaya, who guards the hearth and the hold, and gave the Dawi their runes. Which will it be?
Grimnir the Fearless.
Grungni the Maker.
Valaya of the hearth.
The gods can carve their own statues.

The galleries of your mine were old and badly propped, and the miners were taking ever longer to reach the good seams. You have cut new galleries and new shafts, and shored them up in stone. The ore is coming up faster than ever.
Good stone, good ore.

Word of your work has reached the Masons' Guild, and the guild masters have come to see it for themselves. They walked through your halls for a whole day without saying a word. At the end of it they named you a master mason, and asked if you would take an apprentice.
A master of the oldest craft.

You have planned a new throne hall for years: a hall cut deep into the mountain, its roof held up by pillars carved as the kings of your clan, its floor laid in patterns of red and black stone. It would be the work of a lifetime, and it would be talked of in every hold of the Karaz Ankor.
Cut it to last ten thousand years.
A plain hall, well cut, will do.

The masons have suggested, and they are not wrong, that the new hall needs a great statue. Who better than its lord? A likeness of you, three times the height of a Longbeard, standing at the head of the hall for every guest to see.
Carve me as I am, but taller.
Carve my ancestors instead. They earned it.

[dawi_mason_rival.GetTitledName] has insulted you once too often. And [dawi_mason_rival.GetSheHe] is a mason, so proud of [dawi_mason_rival.GetHerHis] statues that [dawi_mason_rival.GetSheHe] talks of nothing else. A few hammer blows in the night, and all that work would be gravel.
Fetch me a hammer.
That is beneath a Dawi.
[dawi_mason_rival.GetFirstName] will find [dawi_mason_rival.GetHerHis] workshop in pieces

You came down to your workshop this morning and found it full of broken stone. Every statue you have carved for the last twenty years has been smashed where it stood: the warriors, the kings, the Ancestor Gods. Somebody came in the night with a hammer and did not leave until the work was done.
MY STATUES!
Find who did this. It goes in the book.
The trail leads to [From.GetTitledName]
Whoever did it covered their tracks

Word has spread through the court: [From.GetTitledName] went down to [From.GetHerHis] workshop and found every statue smashed. They say [From.GetSheHe] sat down among the broken stone and did not speak for a day. You find it hard to keep a straight face.
Such a shame.

[dawi_mason_victim.GetTitledName] is in the hold, and tomorrow [dawi_mason_victim.GetSheHe] is to be shown the new galleries. You know those galleries. You know which props carry the roof, and which ones could be loosened in the night so that the roof would come down at the lightest touch. A fall of rock in the deeps is a sad thing, but nobody would call it murder.
Loosen the props.
Not like this.
[dawi_mason_victim.GetFirstName] goes down into the galleries tomorrow

You were halfway along the new gallery when the roof came down. You heard the props crack and threw yourself forward, and the rock buried the place where you had been standing a heartbeat before. The miners dug you out by lamplight, battered but alive.\n\nThe miners say the props were sound when they set them.
That was no accident.
You find out who loosened the props: [From.GetTitledName]
You were halfway along the new gallery when you heard the props crack above you. There was no time to run.

The roof came down in the new gallery just as you had planned, but [From.GetTitledName] was quicker than you thought. The miners dug [From.GetHerHim] out alive, and now they are asking how sound props came to crack.
Next time.

The roof came down in the new gallery just as you had planned. It took the miners two days to dig out what was left of [From.GetTitledName]. Everybody says what a terrible accident it was, and you agree with them.
The deeps are dangerous.

It has been a long week of petitions, accounts and grudges, and from the tavern below the hall you can hear singing. A Dawi lord can go down and drink with his people now and then without losing his dignity. Mostly.
I will!
Not tonight.
I have work to do.
You go down to the tavern
The Tavern

The tavern is warm and loud and smells of ale, pipe smoke and roasting meat. In one corner a table of miners is singing about a troll that ate a cart. By the fire sit a party of umgi traders from somewhere far away, haggling over their supper. And at the long table the drinking Dawi have already called for their third cask.
A quiet corner, and a flagon.
Sit with the umgi traders.
Join the drinking Dawi.

An old Longbeard with a scarred face and a beard to his belt sits down across from you without asking. He has been everywhere, he says: the Badlands, the high passes, the lost holds of the east. He looks into his empty flagon meaningfully.
Buy him another, and let him talk.
Leave me be, old one.
He has tales to tell

The Longbeard talks until the fire burns down: of the wars against the grobi in the Badlands, of a dragon he saw over Karak Vlag, of the halls of Karak Eight Peaks with the Skaven running in them. He has no clan left to go home to, he says at last. He has outlived them all.
Then stay at my hold. There is always room for a Longbeard.
A fine tale. Safe roads to you, old one.

You meant to have one flagon in a quiet corner. Then you had another. Somewhere around the sixth the room began to turn, and you have just knocked a whole tray of flagons off the table with your elbow. Everybody is looking at you.
Another round, on me!
That is enough for one night.

[dawi_tavern_friend.GetTitledName] has come down to the tavern as well, and sees you sitting alone. [dawi_tavern_friend.GetSheHe] comes over with two flagons and asks if [dawi_tavern_friend.GetSheHe] may join you.
Sit, and drink.
I want to drink alone.

One of the umgi traders has a book he swears was written by a Dawi, a lost work of the ancestors that he picked up in a market far to the south. The runes on the cover look right, at least in the firelight. He wants twenty-five gold for it, and will not take less.
I will take it.
It is obviously a forgery.
The book is genuine
The book is a forgery
The book is genuine: a reckoner's notes from the days of the first holds, full of things the Dawi had forgotten. You have read it twice already, and every time you find something new.
Worth every coin.
The book is a forgery. The runes on the cover are right, but inside it is umgi scribbling dressed up in Khazalid letters, and some of it is upside down. The traders left town the morning after.
If I ever see that trader again...
The traders tell you about their homeland far away: its cities and its kings, its wars and its strange gods. Half of it is lies, but the other half is worth hearing.
Tell me more.
The traders are hungry for Dawi goods: good steel, good tools, good ale. By the end of the evening you have struck a bargain that will fill your coffers nicely.
A good bargain.

The traders turn out to be agents of a manling bank, hunting [dawi_debtor.GetTitledName], who owes them a great deal of money. They say there is a reward for anyone who can tell them where to find [dawi_debtor.GetHerHim].
I know where [dawi_debtor.GetSheHe] is.
A Dawi does not inform for umgi.

The Dawi at the long table are singing the old songs of the hold, and you sing with them until your throat is raw: songs of the first kings and the great halls, of grudges and vengeance, and of the gold that lies in the deep places. By the end the whole tavern is on its feet.
Another! The one about the troll!

One of the drinking Dawi turns out to be good company: he can drink almost as much as you, tell a story well, and he does not mind losing at dice. By the end of the night you are calling each other kin.
Come and see me at the hall.
A big miner at the long table bangs his flagon down and challenges anyone in the tavern to outdrink him. Every eye in the room turns to you.
Bring the ale!
Not tonight.
You win the contest
You lose the contest
Twelve flagons in, the miner slides slowly off his bench and under the table, and the tavern roars. You are still on your feet. Just.
Who is next?
You remember the eighth flagon. You do not remember the ninth. You wake up under the table with the miner's boots in your face, and the whole tavern knows it.
Never again.

You are a beardling no longer. The clan has gathered in the hall to see you take your place among the adults of the hold, and the eldest of the clan's women has given you the keys of your own hearth, as they were given to her.
Valaya watch over my hearth.

Every Dawi of the hold must take up arms for it, and the time has come for you to choose your weapon. The crossbow of the Quarrellers, which the Dawi have carried since the first holds. The axe and shield of the clan warriors, who stand in the line. Or the handgun of the Thunderers, the new weapon of the Engineers, which the old Dawi do not trust.
The crossbow. I will be a Quarreller.
Axe and shield. I will stand in the line.
The handgun. I will be a Thunderer.
I want no part of it.
A Slayer has only one path.
You begin your training
Training Begins

At dawn you join the other young Quarrellers at the butts below the hold. The drill master is a Longbeard who has carried a crossbow for two hundred years. He hands you yours and tells you that if you drop it, he will drop you.

At dawn you join the other young warriors on the practice ground. The drill master is a scarred old veteran who has stood in the shield wall against every enemy the Dawi have. He hands you an axe and a shield, and the beating begins.

At dawn you join the other young Thunderers at the range below the hold. The drill master is an old Thunderer with burn scars on both hands. He hands you a handgun and a powder horn, and tells you which end to point at the grobi.
I am ready.
The training goes well
The training goes badly
Your bolts and balls are finding the mark more often than not, and the drill master has stopped shouting at you. That, the others tell you, means he is pleased.

You have learned to hold your place in the shield wall when the veterans come at you, and to strike over the rim of your shield. The drill master has stopped knocking you down, which the others tell you means he is pleased.
Only a little longer.
You will be sworn to the ranks
It is not going well. Your shots go wide, your feet go the wrong way, and the drill master has started calling you wazzock in front of the others.
I will try harder.
The drill master will judge you
In the hall, before your clan, you swear to stand with the Quarrellers in the defence of the hold, and to carry the crossbow of your ancestors until you can carry it no more.
In the hall, before your clan, you swear to stand in the shield wall in the defence of the hold, and not to break while a single Dawi stands beside you.
In the hall, before your clan, you swear to stand with the Thunderers in the defence of the hold, and to keep your powder dry and your aim true.
For the hold, and the ancestors!

The drill master has made his judgement before the whole practice ground: you are not fit to stand with the others. A Dawi who cannot fight for his hold has failed his clan, and you will hear about it for the rest of your life.
I have shamed my clan.
The Warriors Guild will let you try again

You have stood in the line for the hold for longer than most Dawi live. Your beard is long and grey, and the young warriors look to you. Now the time has come to take your place among the veterans: with the Longbeards, who keep the old ways and remember every grudge, or with the Ironbreakers, who hold the Underway against the grobi and the Skaven in the dark.
With the Longbeards.
With the Ironbreakers.

Before the whole hall you kneel to [Root.Liege.GetTitledName] and swear the Hammerer's oath: to guard [Root.Liege.GetHerHim] with your life, to stand at [Root.Liege.GetHerHis] side in every battle, and to die before [Root.Liege.GetSheHe] does.

Before the whole hall you kneel to [Root.Liege.GetTitledName] and swear the Hammerer's oath: to guard [Root.Liege.GetHerHim] with your life, to stand at [Root.Liege.GetHerHis] side in every battle, and to die before [Root.Liege.GetSheHe] does.\n\nThen [Root.Liege.GetSheHe] gives you the great hammer that is the Hammerer's sign. It was forged in the hold's own forges, and it is heavier than any you have ever held.
My life is yours.
You are no longer one of your lord's Hammerers. You have handed back your place in the guard, and gone back to the ranks of the clan warriors.
So be it.
The enemy came on in a howling mass, and the line held. You were in the front rank, axe and shield, and you did not take a step back all day.
The enemy charged straight at your Thunderers, and you held your fire until you could see their teeth. Then the volley went off like a thunderclap.
The enemy champion came striding through the press, cutting down Dawi as he came. You wound your crossbow, took aim, and waited for the gap.
For the ancestors!
You win honour in the fighting
You win the fight, but not without a wound
Through the smoke you see [dawi_saved_kin.GetTitledName] cut off from the line, alone, and the enemy closing on [dawi_saved_kin.GetHerHim] from three sides. There is no time to call for help.
Hold on, I am coming!

You were cut off from the line and surrounded, and you had made your peace with the ancestors. Then [From.GetTitledName] came through the enemy like a miner through soft rock, and dragged you back to the shield wall. You owe [From.GetHerHim] your life.
I will not forget this.
Between volleys you and [dawi_shooting_rival.GetTitledName] have been keeping count of your kills, shouting the tally across the firing line. The enemy did not stand long against the two of you.
I make it nine to your eight.
Between volleys you and [From.GetTitledName] have been keeping count of your kills, shouting the tally across the firing line. The enemy did not stand long against the two of you.
Nine? I counted ten!

You and [dawi_longbeard_kin.GetTitledName] stood side by side in the line, two old beards who have fought more battles than either can remember. The young warriors watched how you did it, and did the same.
Just like old times.
You and [From.GetTitledName] stood side by side in the line, two old beards who have fought more battles than either can remember. The young warriors watched how you did it, and did the same.
We are not dead yet.
The Hammerers went in where the fighting was thickest, their great hammers rising and falling like the hammers of a forge, and the enemy line broke in front of them.
Nothing stands before the Hammerers!

The warriors of the court gathered round the fire last night and talked over old battles: who stood, who ran, who should have been there. Every one of them remembers it differently, and every one of them is certain.
It was I who held the bridge!
[dawi_sparring_partner.GetTitledName] is on the practice ground with axe and shield, and asks if you would care to try a few passes.
[dawi_sparring_partner.GetTitledName] is at the butts with a target set up, and asks if you would care to shoot a few rounds.
Gladly.
Another day.

[dawi_shooting_rival.GetTitledName] has been saying again that the crossbow was good enough for the ancestors and the handgun is a smoking toy for engineers. Every Thunderer in the court has heard about it, and they are all looking at you.

[dawi_shooting_rival.GetTitledName] has been saying again that the crossbow is a relic and the handgun is the weapon of the future. Every Quarreller in the court has heard about it, and they are all looking at you.
Settle it at the butts.
An old quarrel. Let it lie.
You win the match
You lose the match
You have carried the crossbow all your life, as your father did and his father before him. Now word comes that [From.GetFirstName] has chosen the handgun of the Thunderers.
You have carried the handgun of the Thunderers all your life. Now word comes that [From.GetFirstName] has chosen the old crossbow of the Quarrellers.
No son of mine!
It is his life.

A letter from your father, [From.GetTitledName]. He has heard of the weapon you chose. He writes that it is not the one he would have picked, but that he will be proud of you as long as you carry it well.
Thank you, father.

A letter from your father, [From.GetTitledName]. He has heard of the weapon you chose, and he writes that you have shamed the clan, that no son of his would carry such a thing, and that he does not wish to see you at his table.
Then he will not.
[From.GetFirstName] is gone. Your son took his things in the night and left your court, and has not said where he is going. The whole hold is talking about it.
He will come back.

A Blood Grudge against [grudge_offender.GetBestName] is written in the Book of Grudges of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName]. No gold can strike it out: only [grudge_offender.GetHerHis] death, or [grudge_offender.GetHerHis] Slayer oath.
Every grudge of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] against [grudge_offender.GetBestName] is struck out, Blood Grudges too.
The Blood Grudge against [This.GetBestName], written in red, still unsatisfied
A public apology, before [grudge_offender.GetHerHis] whole court.
[grudge_offender.GetHerHisCap] head, or [grudge_offender.GetHerHis] Slayer oath.

The Reckoner comes back to say it is done: [From.GetBestName] stood up before [From.GetHerHis] own court and took back every word. The grudgekeeper writes the day in the last column and draws a line through it.

A Reckoner of Clan [From.GetOnlyDynastyName] stands before your court with a stone tablet under his arm. You insulted [From.GetTitledName], he says, and a Dawi does not forget an insult. But Dawi law is fair: a slight is paid with words. Take back what you said, here, before your court, and the grudge is struck out.
Very well. I take it back.
I meant every word.

A Reckoner of Clan [From.GetOnlyDynastyName] stands before you, and the tablet under his arm is cut in red. It is a Blood Grudge, he says, and blood does not wash out with gold. Give yourself up to the justice of [From.GetTitledName], or go to the shrine of Grimnir, shave your head and swear the Slayer's oath, and seek a death that will wipe the debt away.

A Reckoner of Clan [From.GetOnlyDynastyName] stands before you, and the tablet under his arm is cut in red. It is a Blood Grudge, he says, and blood does not wash out with gold. [From.GetTitledName] demands nothing less than that you give yourself up to Dawi justice. The Reckoner does not seem to expect you to agree.
I will take the Slayer's oath.
I give myself up.
Tell your master to come and take my head, if he can.

[From.GetTitledName] has come to your hold in chains of [From.GetHerHis] own choosing and knelt before your throne. The Blood Grudge of Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] can be struck out with a single stroke of the axe.
Fetch the headsman.
Let [From.GetHerHim] rot in a cell instead.

Word comes from the shrine of Grimnir: [From.GetTitledName] has shaved [From.GetHerHis] head, put aside [From.GetHerHis] lands and kin, and sworn the Slayer's oath. [From.GetSheHeCap] will seek [From.GetHerHis] death against the worst foes of the Dawi. By the old law that is enough, and the Blood Grudge is struck out.
Grimnir grant [From.GetHerHim] a worthy death.

[From.GetTitledName] is dead, and it was Clan [Root.GetOnlyDynastyName] that killed [From.GetHerHim]. The grudgekeeper brings out the book, writes the day in the last column, and draws a line through the entry, slowly and with great satisfaction.
Struck out at last.

[From.GetTitledName] is dead, but not by your hand, and [From.GetSheHe] never made amends. By Dawi law a debt does not die with the one who owes it: the grudge passes to [dawi_grudge_heir.GetTitledName], and the grudgekeeper writes the new name beside the old.
Then the heir will pay.
Your grudges against [From.GetBestName] pass to [dawi_grudge_heir.GetBestName]. A Blood Grudge passes as a grudge of war.

The priests of Gazul have sealed [From.GetTitledName] in the clan vault, and [From.GetSheHe] has gone to the Halls of the Ancestors with grudges still open in [From.GetHerHis] book. The old Dawi say such a soul is seated far down the feasting table, away from the great ancestors, with poor food and thin ale. Until you settle what [From.GetSheHe] left unsettled, the shame is yours to carry.
I will settle every one of them.
You take up every grudge in [From.GetFirstName]'s book. Settle any one of them to lift the shame.
A Grudge Avenged
A grudge has been struck out of the clan's book, and the deed written in the Book of Remembrance for the Day of Remembrance.
Far from the Ancestors
A parent went to the Halls of the Ancestors with a grudge unsettled, and sits far from the ancestors' table until it is settled.
Far from the Ancestors
A parent went to the Halls of the Ancestors with several grudges unsettled, and sits far from the ancestors' table until they are settled.
Far from the Ancestors
A parent went to the Halls of the Ancestors with a Blood Grudge or a book full of grudges unsettled, and sits at the very foot of the ancestors' table until they are settled.
[grudge_offender.GetSheHeCap] will swear the Slayer oath, and Grimnir will judge [grudge_offender.GetHerHim].
